context: The problem is still to count ways to climb the stairs, taking 1 or 2 stairs per move. The base cases are dp[1] = 1 and dp[2] = 2. Memoized search uses an array mem to store computed values for nonbase states. A base case returns immediately. For any other state, check the cache first and recurse only if there is no entry.
description: The first-time computations follow the main chain dp[9] → dp[8] → dp[7] → … → dp[3]. An ellipsis stands for dp[6] through dp[4] along the way. The state dp[3] then splits into the base cases dp[2] and dp[1]. On the right, scissors explicitly mark reuse of the cached values dp[7], dp[6], and dp[5]. Ellipses summarize the remaining reuse. Following the code through the omitted section, dp[6] also reuses dp[4], and dp[5] reuses dp[3]. The right subproblem of dp[4], namely dp[2], returns directly as a base case and is not a cache hit.

For example, to compute dp[9], first complete the left subproblem dp[8]. In doing so, the search computes and stores dp[7]. When it then reaches the right subproblem (dp[7], marked with scissors), it reads the cached value without expanding the state again. The value still contributes to the sum for dp[9].
The first table lists the three instances of reuse explicitly marked in the figure. The second explains how the code handles a base case, a first computation, and a cache hit.

frames.explanation: Each nonbase state is expanded and computed only once. Repeat requests return the cached value directly, reducing the time complexity to O(n).
frames.title: Reusing computed states in memoized search

summary: The search first computes and caches subproblems along the main chain on the left. When a state recurs on the right, the search returns its cached value and uses it in the parent state's sum.
